The study demonstrates the effectiveness of this method in predicting future medicine use and its ability to reduce the error rate in identifying animals that may respond poorly to specific drugs.

We introduce a novel approach to reasoning using a dataset called ATOMIC, an Atlas of Machine Common Knowledge. Existing works, such as MSCOCO and ImageNet, focus on describing individual images or scenes but fall short in capturing the broader common knowledge between people and the world around them. Our ATOMIC dataset overcomes this limitation by compiling a vast amount of descriptive information on the relationships between objects, objects and images, and objects and other objects. We demonstrate our approach with a range of pre-trained models and develop three additional tasks, including predicting everyday common sense, understanding the world through graph-based representations, and reasoning about the connections between entities. Our results indicate that using ATOMIC enables the creation of machine models that can reason about the world in a more human-like manner.

This study presents NISQ-HHL, a new quantum portfolio optimization algorithm, which leverages the HHL system of linear equations solver. By utilizing a highly efficient solver, NISQ-HHL can potentially solve large-scale portfolio problems with a significantly smaller number of iterations, thus avoiding the limitation of precision in variational algorithms. We validate the performance of NISQ-HHL through hardware simulations, demonstrating its portfolio selection capabilities and computational advantages over classical solvers and the Variational Quantum Eigensolver-based portfolio optimization method.

Recently, pre-trained language models have significantly advanced NLP tasks.
To leverage their potential in speech-related NLP applications, we introduce a novel training approach, called the speech-text oriented bidirectional focus (STBF) loss, which allows for the seamless integration of audio signals and textual content.
By implementing our method on a basic multi-modal training framework, we can effectively enforce consistency between text and speech signals and enhance speech recognition performance.
Experiments conducted on the Librispeech dataset demonstrate that our proposed loss function outperforms the unimodal baseline and achieves comparable results to the high-performance speech recognition system known as FBank+BERT.
Furthermore, our results indicate that pre-training language models with multimodal input signals yields substantial benefits.

The problem of the average cross section was initially addressed by P. Gruber in 1967, and this study continues that work by applying new mathematical tools to prove the existence of areas with a stationary average cross section. Additionally, this study reveals that such areas include triangles as a subset of possibilities.

As the size $n$ increases, the probability that a random function from the set of permutations of $1$ to $n$ to the set of integers from $1$ to $n$ is considered a parking function of type $k$ converges to a specific probability $p_k$ for any non-negative integer $k$. Furthermore, the sum of initial positions for all uniform random parking functions of type $k$ within the set of permutations of $1$ to $n$ to the set of integers from $1$ to $n$ will, when divided by $n$, approach the value that maximizes the expression $x\ln x - (k+1)x\ln(x-1) + (k+1)(x-1)\frac{x-2}{x-1} - x + 1$ as $n$ approaches infinity.

Researchers investigated the electrical properties of superconducting NbN nanowires, which were so narrow that their resistance was influenced by quantum effects. A study found that when a voltage was applied across the wires, they exhibited a unique behavior where the resistance decreased and then increased gradually. This pattern was similar in both narrow and wider wires, but the rate of increase was faster in narrower wires. A theoretical model was able to accurately predict this unique resistance pattern, showing that it was caused by quantum phase slips, which are fluctuations in the superconducting state. This finding provides valuable insights into the quantum behavior of superconducting materials and their potential applications in next-generation electronic devices.

The initial discovery of a T-dwarf, GJ 229B, in 1996, was a significant milestone in the field of astronomy. Since then, the understanding of this substellar object has been primarily based on the analysis of its spectrum, which has been complicated by the limited availability of theoretical models capable of accurately describing T-dwarf spectra. In this context, we utilized the new generation of the EXOplanet 2050+ retrieval code, APOLLO, to develop a series of sophisticated atmospheric models for GJ 229B. These models, which were constrained by the latest measurements of the object's physical properties, revealed the presence of carbon monoxide and methane in the atmosphere, as well as the existence of thermal disequilibrium. Furthermore, the analysis of the atmosphere's chemical composition indicated an unusually high abundance of carbon, which was also observed in other T-dwarfs. To gain further insights into this anomaly, we conducted an exploration of the atmosphere's vertical structure, which was complicated by the lack of a comprehensive treatment of non-local thermodynamic equilibrium effects in the atmosphere.

The nature of the quark-gluon medium is extensively studied through the observation of short-lived particle decays, such as vector meson decays into two photons, which provide a double radiative signature. A comprehensive analysis of a vector meson's interaction with the quark-gluon medium is presented, revealing that the dominant scattering processes are radiative in nature. These interactions result in the absorption and re-emission of photons and partons by the vector meson, leading to its diffusion within the medium. Notably, scattering with photons and partons occurs on comparable scales, underscoring the importance of including both in any theoretical model. A key finding is that the vector meson's mean free path is primarily determined by gluon scattering, which also influences its radiative energy loss. A distinct two-scale structure of the quark-gluon medium relative to the vector meson is described, consisting of a region of partonic scattering and a broader region of photonic scattering. This has significant implications for the design of optimal final states for detecting vector mesons in future experiments.

Predicting future images in a driving scenario is a crucial task for creating advanced driving systems. This study explores an underutilized camera perspective, such as side and rear-mounted cameras, to enhance the reliability of forecasting. We propose an innovative approach that leverages this supplementary view by initially predicting the central view based on the side view, followed by predicting the central view in the subsequent frames. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of this two-stage representation method compared to direct modeling, yielding improved performance metrics including PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS.

The Hubbard model, a key theoretical framework in condensed matter physics, is known for its interplay between different electron orbitals due to interaction. This study presents the first experimental observation of inter-orbital effects using a highly precise optical trap that confines two distinct atom populations. By applying a magnetic field, we induce a coupling of specific electron orbitals and measure the impact of their interaction on stability. Our findings reveal a significant reduction in the critical density at which atoms transition to a non-equilibrium state as the degree of orbital mixing increases, providing a direct and quantifiable indication of inter-orbital interaction within distinct atom subspaces.

The Ω-baryon, containing three strange quarks, is an ideal candidate for 
research using spectroscopic techniques, particularly the study of the S-wave 
and 3Q-spin alignment of the s-quarks in the ${}^4S_{3/2}$ state. This analysis 
is being conducted to investigate the $\Omega^-$ baryon's spectrum, with a 
focus on comparing theoretical predictions to experimental data from the 
Belle collaboration. Our predictions for key mass parameters, including total 
mass, spin, and fragmentation behavior, are in reasonable agreement with 
observed values. Notably, the predicted mass of the $\Omega_b^-$ baryon falls 
outside the detection range of the Belle collaboration, yet it can potentially 
be detected by the LHC collaboration.

Public transportation systems, especially in densely populated urban areas, serve as a significant means of travel that can also contribute to the dissemination of infectious diseases.  Research into the transmission of illnesses on public transportation has been conducted using various models, and a key challenge lies in accounting for the complex and ever-changing interactions between passengers during their journeys.  A key feature of such models should be a flexible framework that can accurately capture the dynamics of disease transmission in shared spaces with limited airflow.  A crucial aspect of researching this topic is to establish a clear understanding of the benefits and constraints of adopting a mixed distribution approach.  A crucial finding of this research is that utilizing a mixed distribution approach to model the spread of illnesses on urban buses can yield more accurate predictions of disease prevalence than alternative methods.  A crucial recommendation of the authors is to further investigate the use of this approach to improve predictions of illness spread in other shared spaces in urban areas.

Evaluating quantum vacuum birefringence and light-to-force effects demands detecting minute changes in patterns of particles that have undergone diffraction.  We propose using the diffraction pattern as a detection method for quantum vacuum effects, and analyze the difference in how photons with different polarizations are affected.  These differences result in shifted diffraction patterns that can be detected.  Our findings show that the magnitude of the shift for QB forces is too small to be noticeable, and the effect's dependence on length makes it difficult to detect using a wide range of detector geometries.  However, the bE effect can be detected by using a specific detector with a particular geometric configuration.

This paper presents an innovative technique to determine complete transitivity
for any polyhedron defined by convex hulls. By utilizing this technique, we
achieve several notable results: first, we establish that any 4-homosederiv
polyhedron is inherently completely 4-transitive. Secondly, we provide explicit
definitions for all permutahedra of dimension less than or equal to 6, proving
that all such permutahedra are completely flag-transitive. Finally, we establish
that any trivalent polyhedron whose facets are permutahedra is completely
transitive.

We revisit the concepts of unforgeable encryption and authentication within the framework of CQPT and quantum PT systems, revealing that unforgeable encryption is only feasible in classical PT systems, whereas in CQPT systems, the Notarized Mac-Encrypt scheme successfully achieves unforgeable encryption and authentication.

Physical layer authentication has emerged as a promising keyless verification technique, with research primarily centered on developing secure and efficient protocols. To assess the performance of these protocols in practical scenarios, comprehensive simulation studies are necessary. This research presents an efficient keyless verification protocol and conducts thorough simulations to evaluate its security and performance characteristics. Our results demonstrate that the proposed language-based method effectively distinguishes between legitimate and fraudulent transmissions without compromising confidentiality, while also being computationally feasible. Additionally, the study reveals that the efficiency of the proposed method can be enhanced by adjusting the observation period, with the optimal balance between security and verification speed achieved at an observation period of 0.1 seconds.

We've analyzed the flat-band surface plasmon polariton (FB-SPP) mode in twisted transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), specifically in $\theta$-MoS$_2$ and $\theta$-WS$_2$. Our study reveals that the FB-SPP mode can be sustained across a broad range of twist angles, from 0$^{\circ}$ to 30$^{\circ}$. Moreover, we've discovered that the FB-SPP mode exhibits robustness against variations in twist angle, layer configuration, and TMD type. By numerically calculating the FB-SPP mode's characteristics, we've obtained its corresponding FB-SPP spectrum. Our findings demonstrate that the FB-SPP mode in twisted TMDs exhibits remarkable stability and versatility.

This research paper examines the properties of a specific type of geometric structure called a nontrivial nearly conformal Ricci soliton when placed on a Sasakian manifold. We demonstrate that if this soliton coexists with a harmonic map, it must take on a 'gradient' form. Additionally, if a Ricci soliton that is 'almost conformal' is found on a cosymplectic manifold and is also in a 'harmonic map' relationship, it necessarily becomes a soliton that is 'conformal' by nature. Finally, we establish that if a Ricci soliton that is 'almost conformal' is discovered as a quotient space of a hyperbolic space, it must take on a 'gradient' form.

This study provides an overview of how stellar winds from G-type stars impact their systems, in contrast to the effects of massive O and M-type stars. The analysis also covers how these influences affect terrestrial planets, gas giants, and other celestial bodies. The distinct characteristics of O, G, and M stars, along with their respective lifespans and levels of radiation, are explored. The discussion highlights the differences in coronal mass ejections and their effects on gas giants like Jupiter, in comparison to terrestrial planets with active magnetospheres like Earth and Jupiter, and bodies with induced magnetospheres like Mars, Venus, and moons such as Io, Phobos, and Deimos. The study provides insights into the effects of stellar radiation on the habitability of exoplanets.

Spin-orbit proximity effect is crucial in creating high-quality two-dimensional systems with strong spin-orbit coupling through the interaction of layers with and without the effect. The magnitude of the effective Hamiltonian in a thin magnetic film is determined by the material's thickness and scattering at the boundary. This study focuses on a thin magnetic Cobalt layer situated beneath a thin non-magnetic Bismuth layer, examining the effective Hamiltonian in both layers. The spin-splitting in the Bi layer's bands is influenced by the Cobalt layer, and a large spin-mixing rate is observed near the boundary in the Co layer. The effective spin-orbit coupling in the Bi layer is found to be about 1.4 meV, and an anomalous Hall effect of about 1.4 x 10^4 T^-1 is observed in a mesoscopic Bi/Co sample.

This paper utilizes the Jumarie type fractional derivative to solve the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation associated with a generalized Mie-like potential in multiple dimensions. By applying the semi-itinerant variational iteration method, we successfully obtain approximate solutions for the problem.

To prevent overfitting in neural networks, a statistical learning theory approach is proposed, specifically adapting the Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension and covering number concepts. This theoretical framework suggests that restricting a neural network's rate of change, or Lipschitz consistency, can significantly enhance its generalization capabilities. The new hypothesis posits that models adhering to this consistency will be more robust. The proposed regularization technique is integrated into the neural network's loss function, enabling the use of existing optimization tools for efficient training. The resulting method is demonstrated to be computationally feasible and effective, yielding improved performance on both synthetic and real-world datasets, including MNCE and CIFAR-10. The results further reveal that enforcing this regularization technique yields not only better generalization but also increased noise resilience and covering capacity.

Neural machine translation has seen significant performance improvements,
acquiring the ability to replicate linguistic phenomena like agreement.
Although the mechanism behind this replication remains unclear, we found that
LSTM-based models excel at capturing agreement, particularly in Basque.
Our experiments revealed that these models can effectively capture the necessary
information for accurate translation, even when it appears to contradict
universal principles of processing. Moreover, we discovered that they can also
acquire the mechanism of working memory, enabling them to replicate agreement
without relying on its cognitive underpinning.

Astronomers have developed advanced methods to explore exoplanets using the James Webb Space Telescope. Precise timing information, or an accurate ephemeris, is crucial for this, especially for observing the transit of exoplanets. In this study, we used a global network of telescopes to refine the transit schedule for exoplanet HD 80606 b and demonstrate that even rare transits can yield valuable information. Our observations detected a rare "grazing" transit, confirming previous findings and providing a more precise transit duration prediction for its next major transit in 2027. This next transit will be ideal for detailed study with the transit method and potentially with radial velocity measurements. Our research highlights the value of observing rare transits and the importance of precise ephemerides in exoplanet research.

The success of video game-based therapy relies on incorporating personal preferences into treatment plans, as research into how people interact with games can inform the creation of rehabilitation software. This study aims to utilize statistical modeling of user gameplay to guide the development of therapy software for actions requiring coordination between both upper limbs. By utilizing machine learning techniques, a system can be established that classifies coordination patterns and recommends games tailored to enhance specific coordination abilities. Additionally, this research proposes a method for combining the skills of multiple specialized systems, as well as a framework for automatically adjusting game settings to optimize patient engagement.

This paper estimates specific functionals on disjointly fragmented maps within a particular subset of a domain, drawing on Brezis's work from 2003. Brucato, De Rosa, and Novaga build on previous research by Brancatore and Bruschini from 2019, utilizing phase-field techniques. They first establish strong convergence results for sequences of approximations and subsequently prove fractal relaxation theorems.

This study examines the Drell-Yan production of a scalar leptoquark $LQ$ in quark-antiquark annihilation and hadronization at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). We analyze the Drell-Yan process for a scalar $LQ$ with specific decay signatures into a top quark and charm quark, and investigate the impact of higher-order corrections by comparing our results to those obtained through Monte Carlo simulations.

Recent advancements in deep neural networks have significantly reduced scan times for PET by reducing PET images based on CT images. However, this PET reduction process increases the risk of receiving poor-quality images with misleading diagnostic information when encountering new patients that the model has not been trained on. To address this issue, we propose a new approach called Uncertainty-Aware PET-CT Translation (UPCT), which estimates the probability distribution of PET images instead of just predicting reduced images. This approach allows the model to identify and flag low-confidence predictions, thereby minimizing the risk of receiving poor-quality images. By leveraging reduced-dimensional variational inference, our model can efficiently learn complex data relationships and generate high-fidelity PET images. We demonstrate that our reduced model framework can be trained quickly and accurately, even with reduced datasets. Our approach outperforms existing methods by improving both the quality of the generated PET images and the precision of the estimated probability distributions.

This research proposes a unique concept called Customization, Privacy, and Interoperability (CPI) to enhance the user experience in Internet of Things (IoT) systems. We suggest that users should have the freedom to personalize their experiences with smart devices while maintaining control over their data. We developed an innovative framework and system to bring this vision to life. Our approach leverages the power of blockchain technology to provide a secure and transparent platform for users to customize their IoT experiences. We demonstrate our system's effectiveness through a practical implementation, showcasing its ability to provide a safe and user-friendly experience.

This paper centers on the role of Grammatical (or Classical) Theories in the context of coreference resolution using neural networks. To address the current limitations of existing coreference resolution approaches, we aim to integrate a form of centering theory into a state-of-the-art resolution framework. By leveraging centering theory, we can effectively identify potential referents for each expression through the use of neural-annotated linguistic "lists". Furthermore, we introduce a novel model that utilizes a combination of attention-based and list-based mechanisms to determine coreferent connections. This framework can be applied to a variety of relation types, including those that involve multiple antecedents and anti-coreference. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our method over a range of existing coreference resolution approaches.
This paper provides an overview of up-to-date research in parameterized algorithms related to upward planarity.

Configuring a computer system to execute a particular application demands a complex and time-consuming task, which can be extremely frustrating for novice users.
Although there are numerous system setup tools available, they are frequently difficult to use and often require significant user intervention.
To address this challenge, we developed an automated system setup approach that combines multiple configurations to accomplish the same goal, leveraging advanced programming concepts such as meta-reasoning and program synthesis.
Our methodology is versatile, applicable to a broad range of systems and programs, and can be customized to meet specific user requirements.
We demonstrated the practicality of our approach by automating the system setup for several popular machine learning applications, significantly reducing the time and effort required to achieve optimal performance.

The operator expansion method effectively reduces lengthy expressions, which is commonly encountered in quantum field theory calculations. This method has an underlying group theory foundation, centered on Lie algebra. Building upon previous research, we delve into the underlying entangled relationship between the operator expansion and its constituent elements, specifically focusing on Lie algebra and its breaking point. A novel operator-based entropic measure is proposed to quantify this interconnectedness. The feasibility of this measure is demonstrated through its application to SU(2) symmetry, SU(2)xU(1) symmetry, and the Standard Model Lagrangian.

Recent advancements in WiFi sensing technology have shown promise in accurately determining spatial distances between objects, potentially enabling sophisticated applications such as activity recognition and gesture control. However, retrieving 2D/3D coordinate data from WiFi sensing can be a resource-intensive process, especially when employing methods like trilateration. This study focuses on utilizing the WiFi-based range estimation method to retrieve coordinate data and investigates the transferability of this method across different environments. By leveraging machine learning, particularly artificial neural networks, this study demonstrates the feasibility of estimating ranges based on raw WiFi data. Furthermore, it explores the concept of transfer learning, allowing a model trained in one environment to function effectively in another with minimal retraining. This approach significantly reduces the computational overhead associated with running multiple regression models, thereby enhancing the efficiency of WiFi sensing systems.

We employ a semi-analytical method to investigate the stability of a spherical structure composed of self-gravitating particles orbiting a central black hole. 
Our findings diverge from previous studies that relied on idealized assumptions. 
When considering realistic conditions where particles interact through both self-gravity and equation of state forces, the structure's stability is significantly impacted. 
In particular, we identify distinct patterns of stability that are not observed in idealized scenarios. 
These include the formation of Dyson Shells, which are structures composed of multiple coexisting shells of particles that only gravitate, and Nested SHells, which feature a central black hole surrounded by alternating layers of particles that both self-gravitate and occupy distinct orbital resonances. 
Our research provides valuable insights into the complex dynamics of particle systems in the presence of a central black hole and may guide future observational efforts to detect these unique astronomical phenomena.

Enterprises frequently enter into agreements with service providers, utilizing identification markers to monitor and prevent breaches of the service level agreement.  However, the current methods for implementing this identification are costly, vulnerable to manipulation, and require significant human intervention.  We propose a method for detecting service level agreement breaches through a decentralized approach, leveraging peer-to-peer technology and cryptographic techniques.  By integrating this method into a service management system, we can effectively monitor and prevent breaches of the agreement in a cost-effective and secure manner.

A novel method to mitigate beam disruption instability dependence on beam configuration is proposed for energy recovery linacs. This challenge is particularly pressing for damped energy recovery linacs with high energy and short filling patterns. To address this issue, we present a method to optimize transverse beam feedback settings by intentionally introducing beam configuration-specific settings. This approach enables stable operation across various beam configurations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method using an energy recovery linac test facility and a theoretical model based on an ALICE design, confirming its ability to achieve stable operation with distinct beam disruption instability frequencies for different beam configurations.

Scarcity of neutron sources necessitates efficient utilization of available facilities for research. This study introduces a compact, highly sensitive detector capable of capturing all types of neutrons with exceptional completeness. By employing three-dimensional position-sensitive scintillator strips, the detector achieves complete coverage and provides precise reconstruction of interaction positions and directions of neutrons. Utilizing data from the China High Magnetic Field Laboratory, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the design and provide an accurate neutron cross-section measurement of the CH nucleus, yielding a precise value of $\sigma_{\textrm{CH}} = 1.661 \pm 0.006 \pm 0.015$ barns.

To better understand the early stages of planetary formation, researchers need a deeper insight into how dust particles stick together as temperatures rise. We conducted experiments to observe and measure the forces between two flat surfaces in contact with each other, in an environment that mimics a space vacuum. These experiments were also done at elevated temperatures, up to 400 Kelvin, in a gas that contains water, nitrogen, or both. We found that particles stick together more effectively in the presence of water at lower temperatures, but this advantage diminishes as temperatures increase. In a nitrogen atmosphere, particles' sticking strength is significantly reduced as temperatures rise, particularly above 250 Kelvin. This reduction is even more pronounced in the presence of water, which causes particles' ability to stick to each other to decrease by a factor of 100 as temperatures rise from 200 to 400 Kelvin. Furthermore, particles' ability to stick to each other is affected by the speed at which they collide, with this relationship being more significant in a nitrogen atmosphere than in an atmosphere that contains water. These findings have important implications for the formation of planetary building blocks in the warm inner regions of a disk surrounding a young star.

Supervised dimension reduction techniques are commonly employed to enhance
visualization and data interpretation by simplifying complex datasets. Dimension
reduction techniques facilitate a more straightforward examination of datasets by
identifying patterns and relationships among variables. Among these techniques,
the Fisher Discriminant Analysis (FDA) stands out for its effectiveness in
visualization and interpretation. FDA is a widely used technique for creating a
more manageable representation of datasets by simplifying their complex
structure.

However, traditional FDA techniques have limitations when dealing with datasets
that do not conform to linear assumptions. Non-linear FDA methods have been
developed to address this shortcoming, but assessing their performance and
effectiveness can be challenging.

The local Fisher discriminant assessment (LFDA) toolkit has been created to address
this challenge by providing LFDA and FDA visualization and assessment capabilities.
LFDA offers an advantage over traditional FDA methods by accommodating datasets with
a non-linear structure, allowing for more accurate visualization and interpretation.

By utilizing the local Fisher discriminant assessment (LFDA) toolkit, analysts can
assess the performance of LFDA and FDA methods and gain valuable insights into the
underlying patterns and relationships among dataset variables.

Mimicry learning enables a mobile robot to follow another robot's path around obstacles without requiring a pre-mapped route. This research extends previous mimicry learning studies by: (a) allowing the follower to choose any trajectory, (b) having the follower learn the leader's behavior, (c) avoiding obstacles, and (d) accounting for nonlinear rigid constraints. A new method is proposed that meets these requirements, providing the follower with the ability to safely follow the leader while using the observed leader-follower data for improved efficiency. The approach is validated through numerical simulations and physical experiments.

We have calculated the one-loop central-emission vertex for massless external gauge bosons in four dimensions using an $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory. Our derivation is based on an expansion of an eikonal phase, which has been expressed as a color matrix exponential, incorporating a Glauber-Mueller semi-classical component. The eikonal amplitude is then derived by considering a specific $\mathcal{N}=4$ super-Yang-Mills semi-classical amplitude as a starting point.

A novel type of superfluid, belonging to the topological BCS phase with spin-singlet pairing, is identified within the Rashba Hubbard model at the filled-Rashba band edges. A comparison with the spin-orbit-symmetric model reveals that, although the topological gap parameter remains consistent across both models, the pairing symmetry undergoes a transformation due to the absence of symmetry in the spin-orbit-mixed model. Using a tight-binding model that incorporates the Rashba spin-orbit coupling, we investigate how this novel phase responds to an applied magnetic field and demonstrate that it possesses a robust non-zero Chern number, confirming its topological nature.

Using a scanning SQUID technique, we have detected quantized magnetic flux vortices in a high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprate, specifically in Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_{6+\delta}$ thin films. Our findings reveal that at lower magnetic fields, the flux vortices form a lattice structure with a 4:1 aspect ratio, which is stable even at elevated temperatures close to $T_\textrm{c}$. This square grid is maintained by pinning forces, and we estimate the pinning strength to be approximately $10^9$ Oe/cm$^3$. A transition occurs as the magnetic field increases, where the vortex grid transforms into a disordered state. Our study provides the first direct evidence of this grid-to-disorder transition at temperatures near $T_\textrm{c}$ in a high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprate.

We've developed a new model for molten polymers, specifically in stretched and highly flexible states, and found that 'exclusion areas' can significantly reduce the number of available states for the polymer's tail. These areas arise due to the limited space for the tail to move in. Interestingly, we found that in stretched states, the areas that form at the end of the fiber bundle can effectively be ignored. This is because the molten polymer can easily move apart when compressed, creating space for the tail to move in. This behavior can be likened to the 'sandpile model', where the exclusion areas dynamically adjust to the shape of the fiber bundle. This model can be used to better understand the complex movements of polymers in various states.

Given a graph, its linear drawing becomes easier to identify due to a set of resolution vertices known as the metric dimension. Now, we introduce the concept of shortened distance, which is the difference between the distance between two nodes and a fixed integer, and define a subset of nodes that maximizes the information provided by shortened distances, called the shortest metric dimension. Our paper aims to explore and explain the properties of this new concept, and relate it to the traditional metric dimension, while also addressing some specific aspects of cycles and complete graphs.

A study of 4.7 TB of 10-year 2011-2020 Fermi-LAT Data is presented, focusing on 3kHz time series light curves in the 0.1-3GeV energy range. Initially, 10,000 source light curves were examined, and a machine learning method, GBDT, was used to identify 100 variable sources exhibiting significant fluctuations exceeding 10 standard deviations. Extensive cross-references were made with other wavelengths of observation, including X-ray, gamma-ray from the 10-year analysis, GeV gamma-ray, and radio wavelengths. As a result, 80 sources were highlighted exhibiting strong variability across multiple wavelengths. All sky maps were generated for distinct time periods, and significant shifts in source intensity were observed. Notably, source source identified as NGC 4889, previously unidentified as a gamma-ray source, was found to be a new source in the examined period.

A new concept called over serial dictatorship has been introduced, which encompasses all voting systems with the same level of fairness as serial dictatorship but surpasses it by allowing for more flexibility. It has been discovered that a combination of multiple serial dictatorships, possibly occurring at different times, can achieve any systematic method of decision-making that maintains fairness. This finding provides a more diverse range of fair decision-making systems than using just one serial dictatorship. Furthermore, the systems of decision-making that can be obtained through these fair combinations can be identified using specific criteria, which include measures of fairness, efficiency, and the level of influence held by each individual. Theoretical implications of these discoveries are explored, along with suggestions for exploring them empirically.

We developed an algorithm to identify binary asteroids in the Pan-STARRS1 images, which detects pairs of asteroids that orbit each other. Our method scans the PS1 archive for potential candidates and verifies them through statistical analysis, near-infrared imaging, and astrometric observations. By leveraging the PS1 data's extensive coverage and high resolution, our approach significantly expands the known population of binary asteroids and provides valuable insights into their characteristics, contributing to the growing database of such systems observed by the Asteroid Terrestrial-impact Last Alert! system.

This paper proposes a new method for analyzing and assessing a type of model called partially linear regression in the context of network data. Specifically, it focuses on understanding and estimating a model used to study peer influences within networks. The traditional approach to this model involves assuming data from similar network structures are independent, an assumption that is often violated in practice. To address this issue, the paper seeks to develop statistical tests to assess the model's suitability and recover underlying relationships if the initial assumption is found to be invalid. It proposes using data-driven techniques to adaptively create pseudo-samples from data sets, allowing for the application of standard inference methods. The paper illustrates its methodology through an analysis of peer influences on marijuana use among adolescents.

This study introduces novel expressions for the Leibniz rule under the influence of the Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional integral and differential operator. Building upon this, specific applications are derived and demonstrated with illustrative examples.

Variable gains and time-varying disturbances pose significant challenges in the implementation of spatial audio systems, particularly in creating immersive soundscapes in augmented and virtual reality environments. To address this, we explore the variability of signals in different locations within the metaverse, focusing on the asymptotic behavior of adaptive Variable-Disturbance Rejection (VDRE) filters with variable gains. Specifically, we examine the least-squares error of these signals as the amount of data increases, leading to a result that our Variable gains RLS (VDRE) approach matches the optimal performance of an ideal minimum-variance unbiased filter. Furthermore, we apply our findings to the creation of location-based audio systems in the metaverse, presenting a method to efficiently calculate a large set of rejection signals.

In astrophysics, visualizing spectra and imaging data is crucial for data analysis and interpretation.  Advanced visualization is often necessary to accurately interpret the data.  As a community, we've developed a suite of Python tools designed for effective 2D/3D visualization of imaging and spectral data, along with interactive exploration and spectral decomposition visualization using Matplotlib and Plotly.  These tools, available on GitHub and conda-forge, enable seamless visualization on laptops, tablets, and even on the VLT using the CasuLina interface, allowing for a more efficient data analysis process.  A new version of this suite, now available at https://github.com/ahermouanRCSED, offers enhanced functionality and addresses previous issues.  We've also demonstrated the suite's effectiveness by utilizing it to analyze the spectra and imaging data from the VLT survey of the Carina Nebula.

Our analysis of the Southern Atlantic Ocean's opening used a variety of data sources,
including the age and spread of the Central Atlantic Ridge, measurements of ridge offsets,
transform fault orientations, and the orientation of magnetic anomalies near the ridge.
These data were analyzed through multiple methods, including a standard approach, the
Heliocentric approach, and a new method that minimizes anomalies near the ridge.
Three resulting models were compared to a fourth, reference model, which represents the
most accurate description of plate movements based on the available data.
To facilitate this description, we developed a new method for calculating the RMS misfit
of Euler vectors, which is crucial for assessing the quality of any proposed plate
kinematics.
We found that the Southern Atlantic's plate movements can be explained by the rupture
of three fissures, which occurred sequentially and were located in specific areas of the
Central Atlantic Ridge.
These rupture points were located in the Cape Verde Rise, the Rio Grande Rise, and the
South Atlantic Ridge, which occurred at different times and were responsible for the
separation of the African and South American plates.
We also found that the relative rotation of the African and South American plates was
concentrated in specific areas, which can be seen as the result of the concentration of
seismicity in the Central Atlantic Ridge.
This finding has important implications for understanding the plate tectonics of the
Southern Atlantic Ocean.

When using deep learning for medical image segmentation, a significant problem arises due to the scarcity of annotated data. To overcome this limitation, researchers have turned to self-supervised methods that don't require labeled training data. Although impressive progress has been made, current self-supervised approaches struggle with accurate boundary prediction. To address this issue, we propose an innovative information optimization strategy that considers boundary effects. Our method aims to maximize the amount of relevant information in the feature representation by considering both the amount of information and the amount of irrelevant information. We discovered that information about background pixels often leaks into boundary pixels' feature representation, making it difficult to accurately segment them. By designing a specific optimization strategy, we minimize the irrelevant information on boundary pixels and enhance the model's performance. Our method can be applied to any self-supervised segmentation method and yields remarkable results on various benchmark datasets.

The rise of interactive media has sparked significant interest in Artificial Intelligence, leading to a need for robust, human-like systems capable of collaborating with humans on complex, real-world tasks. Taking a leading role in this endeavor, we present a comprehensive set of guidelines for the successful development of interactive, human-centered AI systems. By focusing on a popular role-playing game, Dungeons and Dragons, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. By incorporating basic psychological principles, including Intention understanding and Theory of Mind, we can create a more human-centric AI system. Utilizing state-of-the-art language models, our proposed LEAD agent outperforms existing role-play models and outdoes human participants in terms of enjoyment and leadership qualities. Our research provides a solid foundation for the creation of human-centric AI systems that can collaborate with humans on complex, real-world tasks.

This paper provides a framework for identifying changes in word meaning over time.
By utilizing Wikipedia's rich textual annotations, we can pinpoint shifts in how specific words convey their significance.
To measure this, we employ Google's Term-to-Document model and assess the resulting representations through both human judgment and WordSense Indifference tests.
Our findings reveal that certain words undergo a notable reorientation in their semantic space, with some words adapting to new concepts and others becoming increasingly marginalized.
This research is pioneering, as it is the first to systematically identify and explore the diverse ways in which lexical meanings evolve over time.

We propose a set of novel functions within the parton landscape, specifically perpendicular quasi-parton and parton distribution functions, which incorporate the transverse quench moment. A theoretical framework for calculating these functions is established through the Heisenberg equation of motion, complemented by a first-principles calculation method using the Wilson line formalism. Our research reveals that the pDF PDF acquires a pivotal role in describing the 3D spatial structure of hadrons, with implications for upcoming experiments at the Electron-Ion Collider.

The intricate folding and knotting of proteins are still not fully understood, 
especially given their biological functions. Previous research focused on identifying factors that 
promote knotting and folding, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. 
Now, a new approach is being proposed to shed light on this topic by using the 
topological properties of a protein's native state to guide the analysis of its bending pathways. 
This method was applied to examine a knotted protein called Uch65, and the results revealed 
distinct bending patterns in different parts of the protein chain. 
Specifically, there are separate folded paths leading to the formation of parts of the knot, and 
these paths can be triggered by heating and slowly cooling the protein. 
However, other bending patterns are disrupted during this process and require more energy to reform. 
Thus, the topological approach provides a way to analyze and understand the complexity of a protein's folding and knotting by identifying separate bending pathways in its native state.

To address the discrepancy in the measured value of the Hubble constant, a new theory called Early Dark Energy is being considered. In this study, the influence of EDE on the relationship between the Hubble constant and other cosmological parameters is examined, and its effects on the cosmic expansion history are used to place new constraints on the model. By combining data from the Planck satellite and the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey, the relationship between the Hubble constant and the matter density is analyzed to determine the most likely values of these parameters under different scenarios. It is found that a specific model of EDE can be constrained to a range of values for a key parameter, which in turn places limits on the model's ability to resolve the Hubble constant discrepancy. These constraints are derived using a statistical method called the profile likelihood, taking into account the uncertainties in the data and the model.

We establish that the symplectic homotopy mapping class groups of blown-up $n$-dimensional tori, denoted as $Sp(\check{X}_n,\dot{=})$, possess a structure of a symmetry type. This achievement extends to include a presentation consisting of generators and defining relations for $Sp(\check{X}_n,\dot{=})$, and further, we confirm that a particular subgroup of this group, $M(\check{X}_n,\dot{=})$, is of finite index.

We've analyzed the divergence of a conserved current in a system that's symmetry broken and either relativity-based or not. When a conserved current's expectation value becomes nonzero, a new particle appears whose mass equals the system's symmetry breaking parameter's value. We've found that this particle behaves differently depending on whether the underlying theory's symmetry breaking parameter's value is the same as a particle with twice that mass, which is observed in some theories. This is seen in the case of the pion in quantum chromodynamics and the Higgs boson in the standard model.

Current NLP models excel at making accurate predictions, but understanding how to make them produce desired outputs is a challenging task. Although manipulating input to achieve desired outcomes is a human capability, automating this process with NLP models proves difficult. One effective method to analyze and interpret NLP models is through the use of phrasal counterfactual explanations, which suggest minimal alterations to the explanation target's outcome. However, the existing algorithms for generating these counterfactuals are limited to word-level changes, thus failing to capture more natural alterations. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel counterfactual explanation generation method based on a large language model that utilizes a unique decoding strategy to identify minimal modifications to the input, resulting in desired outcomes. Our experiments demonstrate that this method effectively identifies accurate and accurate counterfactual explanations across various tasks, including sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, and document-level classification.

The Total coloring problem of a graph G involves assigning colors to both vertices and edges such that no adjacent or incident elements share the same color. A summary of a neighbor v's colors can be formed by adding up the colors of adjacent elements. A total coloring that uniquely identifies each vertex through their neighbor color summaries is possible if such a summary is distinct for every vertex. Certain types of circulant graphs, specifically those with four generators based on consecutive integers, have been shown to be feasible for both fair and unique-distinguishing sum colorings of their neighbors under specific conditions. Additionally, it has been established that the minimum number of colors needed for such a coloring is not exceeding the maximum degree plus the smaller of the graph's odd and even maximum values.

The growth of high-quality Heusler films using remote epitaxy on graphene requires a precise balance of thermal energy and atomic momentum, which can be influenced by adjusting the substrate's temperature and the rate at which atoms are deposited. By fine-tuning these parameters, we can optimize the epitaxial relationship between the film and the substrate, resulting in improved crystalline quality. A systematic study was conducted on the effects of remote epitaxy on Mn$_2$IrRh films grown on Al$_2$O$_3$-covered graphene substrates, revealing that increasing the deposition rate leads to better crystalline quality and larger grain sizes. In addition, it was found that the presence of the monolayer of graphene facilitates the incorporation of Ir and Rh atoms into the Heusler lattice, which is otherwise difficult to achieve. By adjusting the deposition rate, we can also control the equilibrium between remote epitaxy and other growth modes, such as van der Waals epitaxy and pinhole growth. These findings provide valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying the growth of complex multilayer films and have implications for the development of novel spintronic devices.

A code is classified as a $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear code if it results from a combined Castagnoli and Ustunel constructions using $\mathbb{Z}_p$ and $\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$. This research explores the parameters that define the size and structure of such codes, specifically focusing on dimension and null space properties. We provide a detailed examination of code characteristics based on these parameters and include a specific example to illustrate our findings.

The process of injecting ideal polymer plugs into a mold follows a distinct profile, 
characterized by an initial acceleration phase, a steady-state phase, and a deceleration phase. 
During the acceleration phase, the plugs experience increasing shear rates, 
causing them to accelerate and fill the mold gradually. 
In the steady-state phase, the polymer plugs maintain a constant shear rate, 
resulting in a uniform injection speed. 
During the deceleration phase, the shear rates increase, 
causing the polymer plugs to decelerate and complete the injection process. 
This three-phase profile is a fundamental aspect of polymer processing, 
with significant implications for the quality and properties of the final product.

A significant portion of modern classification systems are designed to handle multiple labels for each input, yet the level of activity in single-label research remains high. The motivation behind this lies in the relative ease of annotating single-label data compared to more complex multi-label setups, where several labels need to be assigned. The challenge of scaling multi-label systems is compounded by the need for a diverse range of labeled examples to train models capable of generalizing across different label combinations. The proposed approach, called MultiLEACH, utilizes label clusters to facilitate data augmentation and enable the generation of multi-label datasets from single-label labeled data. The technique is demonstrated using the PASCAL VOC 2007 dataset, with encouraging results showing an improvement of 0.5 mAP over data-unaugmented multi-label baselines and a reduction of 50% in the required annotated data.

This research provides a proof that the energy in a certain type of time-dependent model does not increase over time. Specifically, we extend a previous result from an ordinary differential equation to a more complex setting involving function spaces, where a fractional derivative of order between 0 and 1 causes the energy to decrease at an exponential rate.

The Stueckelberg-Feynman formalism, which uses observation operators and status descriptors to construct quantum mechanical systems' state spaces, is mathematically linked to Zermelo's decision theory through a category theory-based mapping of subcategories.

We propose a novel mechanism to explain the unknown origin of high-energy gamma-rays from galaxies. These particles are produced in binary systems consisting of compact stars and nearby galaxies that have magnetic fields. The binary systems possess accretion disks that emit X-rays and radio waves through a process called synchrotron self-absorption. The strong magnetic fields of the compact stars capture these emissions, preventing them from escaping and instead accumulating energy, which eventually leads to gamma-ray emissions via the synchrotron self-curvature process. This process is particularly effective in galaxies of types Sb, Sc, and dE, which have moderate to weak magnetic fields. This mechanism is consistent with current observations of gamma-rays from galaxies and can also be used to study gamma-rays from galaxies of types Sa and earlier, which have extremely strong magnetic fields.

This study examines the key factors influencing the performance of investment portfolios, specifically the allocation of returns across the portfolio and the individual contributions of various investment assets. To effectively analyze this, we utilize a unique data set comprising real-world portfolios from the past 25 years, which includes almost 200,000 instances where portfolios were allocated and generated returns. The review covers the historical returns and risk characteristics of active and passive management strategies, the contributions of market beta and asset selection to overall portfolio returns, and the advantages of rebalancing the portfolio.

This project focuses on categorizing heart sounds into normal and abnormal types using a convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on a limited dataset.  To improve the training data, a technique called additive noise simulation is employed, allowing for the creation of a more extensive dataset.  The study demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach and shows that a CNN can successfully classify heart sounds into their correct groups, even in the presence of noise.

The rise of mobile and wearable technology has enabled individuals to monitor their health and seek assistance from medical professionals through these devices. However, using such technology for medical diagnosis and treatment poses significant privacy risks, as sensitive data collected by these gadgets can be compromised. As a result, researchers have proposed using federated learning to allow multiple entities to collaborate and train a shared model without sharing their data. Although this approach has been successfully applied in certain fields, there are still challenges due to the limited amount of data available on wearable devices. To address this issue, we present FedHealth, a federated transfer learning framework that allows for personalized medical diagnosis and treatment using wearable technology. FedHealth enables users to contribute to a shared knowledge base and benefit from the collective knowledge of others, while maintaining data security. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.

This study compares multiple portfolio optimization methods based on higher-moment criteria, specifically skewness and kurtosis. Various strategies for selecting and weighting elevated moments are examined, and the resulting approaches are evaluated through both numerical simulations and real-world application.

The coincidence dilemma in cosmic ray physics is the discrepancy between the low observed frequency of highly energetic primary particles and the relatively high number of very energetic secondary particles. A conventional explanation posits that the cosmic ray universe is dominated by protons. However, the low number of primary particles can't be solely accounted for by their low charge. The notion of a charge-degenerate cosmic ray universe is therefore insufficient. The notion of highly energetic secondary particles dominating the universe is equally problematic, as it contradicts the conservation of mass and energy. A novel explanation is proposed, suggesting that highly energetic secondary particles are concentrated in localized regions, forming dense, localized "shells" that rotate and collide, creating localized "folds" that contribute to a charge-rich, three-dimensional cosmic ray universe. This explanation is supported by a theoretical framework that incorporates the conservation of charge, mass, and energy. The proposed explanation is further supported by a calculation of the total charge in the universe, which is found to be very low, in line with the observed low frequency of highly energetic primary particles.

This paper presents a new approach to automating software content analysis,
maintaining a consistent interpretation over time. Unlike conventional methods, our
system automatically breaks down complex documents into basic components, eliminating
the need for a human to structure the content. We have developed a versatile,
pre-trained model that utilizes cutting-edge natural language processing techniques
to achieve this. Our framework is readily accessible through a user-friendly web
interface. In our evaluation, our method outperformed a leading alternative in
extracting key information from public takeover notices, with minimal human input.

This paper tackles a control problem where costs change abruptly, considering a specific scenario from a previous study. The main difficulty lies in a feedback control mechanism that requires sudden toggles in response to the process crossing a boundary. To overcome this, we employ compactification techniques to reframe the problem and utilize viscosity solutions to solve it. Our approach enables us to derive solvability for the original problem under certain conditions, a key result achieved by adapting methods from a cited source and adapting it to accommodate discontinuous costs. Our assumptions are purely mathematical, with no need for Lipschitz continuity often found in similar studies.

This paper introduces a novel SUSY leptoquark scenario where the observed charged lepton matter asymmetry can be attributed to the presence of two types of leptoquarks with different charges, specifically $\bar{D}Q$ and $US$. These leptoquarks are predicted to be produced in pairs at the Large Hadron Collider, and due to their differing properties, they can be identified and distinguished from one another. A detailed analysis of their decay pathways shows that they can be observed through certain final state signatures, and based on certain constraints, a minimum leptoquark mass of 1.1 TeV is required. A hypothetical 14 TeV LHC run with 300 $fb^{-1}$ of data has a 90% confidence level of producing a charged lepton matter asymmetry of approximately 10% of the b-quark asymmetry.

Deep learning techniques have significantly advanced the field of Natural Language Processing, with sequence classification and generation techniques now being utilized to create automated assessment tools. Though several evaluation frameworks have been developed in recent years, most generate lengthy explanations that are difficult for average test-takers to comprehend. In this study, we introduce a compact neural network architecture called GSeqGen, which facilitates rapid generation of concise textual feedback through extensive embeddings. GSeqGen outperforms the state-of-the-art model in two distinct test scenarios: generating accurate assessment items and providing succinct explanations. Specifically, GSeqGen excels in these tasks by significantly reducing the number of steps required for sequence generation, while maintaining high accuracy. As a result, GSeqGen has the potential to create more effective automated testing tools that are user-friendly and provide precise feedback.

We have developed a new model that accounts for the radiative transfer and chemical equilibrium of molecular clouds, which can accurately simulate the low-temperature excitation of metastable states in neutral carbon atoms. Our calculations show that carbon lines at 608 and 873 \AA, which are typically ignored, are actually significantly affected by this process. As a result, the intensity of these lines is much lower than expected, which can lead to incorrect estimations of carbon abundance if not properly considered. Our findings also show that the ratio of C I lines to CO emission is a reliable indicator of carbon abundance, which can be used to distinguish between different types of gas in galaxies. This ratio is particularly useful in galaxies with a wide range of metallicity levels, where it can be used to differentiate between gas that is rich in metals and gas that is relatively poor in metals.

We investigate the concurrent resolution of the $B$ anomalies and the recently observed spin alignment discrepancy in hadronic $B$ decays, within the framework of a vector-based interaction between composite particles. A single set of compositeness scales and preform factors is found to be capable of addressing all these discrepancies, albeit with limited flexibility. Our analysis reveals that resolving the spin alignment discrepancy necessitates a significantly higher energy level, exceeding that required for the $B$ anomalies by more than two orders of magnitude. Furthermore, our results indicate that resolving both sets of anomalies with equal energy levels would require a minimum of four separate composite interaction levels.

Given positive integers d and k, we define the arrangement $\mathcal{A}$ as any collection of unit vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$, such that the inner product of distinct elements is strictly less than $-\frac{1}{k-1}$. We demonstrate that if $\mathcal{A}$ has a finite number of elements, then there exists an arrangement $\mathcal{A}'}$ with the same number of elements that maintains its property while having an integer inner product of its distinct elements equal to $-\frac{1}{2}$. Furthermore, we explore additional constructions that satisfy these criteria.

Research in musical instrument classification has primarily focused on capturing instruments within a single category, such as string or woodwind. This study challenges that conventional approach and proposes a novel strategy to develop a comprehensive system capable of identifying a wide range of musical instruments using only a handful of examples. By leveraging pre-trained models and a hierarchical strategy, we explore the potential to enhance the efficiency of inference in the process of instrument classification. Leveraging the inherent structure of instruments, we propose a two-stage approach to reduce the complexity of the task. This strategy divides the problem into two sub-tasks, where the first stage categorizes instruments into broad instrument families, and the second stage performs detailed classification within each category. By combining the power of transfer learning and a hierarchical strategy, we demonstrate that this approach reduces the computational cost of inference and enhances the efficiency of the process.

To facilitate the next generation of NLP advancements in the research domain, we have assembled a comprehensive dataset comprising 16,154 research articles primarily focusing on natural language understanding. This collection encompasses a wide range of tasks including title and abstract summarization, query formation, query expansion, relevant document retrieval, multi-hop retrieval, core contribution identification, question answering, and multi-hop question answering. Notably, this wide-ranging collection is centered around the peer-reviewed research community and may serve as a unifying framework for enhancing NLP within the research domain. Furthermore, we have shared several strategies to leverage this collection to support researchers and have outlined several potential avenues for future exploration.

The precise timing data from pulsars can be utilized to detect gravitational waves from multiple sources, a method that will be fully realized with the next generation of radio telescopes. Researchers have previously predicted the appearance of specific signals within the data, namely the lone pulsar and sky average components, which arise from elliptical binary systems. These components manifest as periodic variations in frequency and phase. In this study, the precision of our measurements for the periodic parameters of the sky average component were determined as $10^{-4}$ and $10^{-3}$ respectively, using a method based on the periodic Doppler shift. A similar approach was applied to the lone pulsar component, and the resulting precision was found to be comparable to previous studies. To accelerate the computation of these parameters, a method based on the maximum likelihood estimator was implemented, allowing for a significant reduction in processing time. With the anticipated improvements in data quality, these parameters will be measured with unprecedented accuracy, paving the way for the detection of subtle periodic patterns that may be obscured by the typical $O(e^{2})$ modulation of amplitude and phase.

We examine the time-evolving sequence of particle velocities in the Asymmetric Simple
Exclusive Random Walk, a system where particles move on a one-dimensional grid
and move at different velocities, interacting through non-crossing movement and
particle swapping based on directional flow. Our analysis reveals that velocity
distributions across any given bond follow a limiting distribution that can be
derived from the original velocity set through a specific filtering process.

As a result of the ongoing SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, researchers around the world are focused on investigating its spread and preventing further outbreaks. Various mathematical models have been employed to study this phenomenon, yet there is still a lack of a comprehensive review that covers key features common to all such models. Existing surveys have primarily concentrated on a limited geographical area or a specific aspect of model development, leaving a gap in our understanding. This paper aims to fill that gap by examining all major mathematical and statistical modelling approaches used during the pandemic, considering their general applicability beyond the current situation. We have investigated the underlying statistical and mathematical models, explored how transmission dynamics are represented, discussed the implementation of spatial and temporal factors, and examined the incorporation of demographic and clinical data. This review is intended to serve as a valuable resource for those involved in modelling outbreaks, providing a framework that can be applied to future situations.

For a Majorana fermion field, the probability distribution of a Majorana number is derived, and its mean and variance can be expressed in terms of a Majorana fraction. Additionally, a connection between the Majorana fraction and the correlation of fermion number densities in a non-Abelian Chern-Simons theory is established. The expected variance of fermion number densities in this theory is found to be proportional to their mean product multiplied by their Majorana fraction, and this proportionality constant is determined. The expectation value of the Majorana fraction is calculated for both the non-Abelian SU(2) and Gaudin-Meirer models, and the resulting values are compared.

Acronyms are frequently encountered in technical and scientific domains, yet their textual form poses challenges in processing and understanding. This issue is compounded by the fact that a single acronym can have multiple meanings, necessitating accurate resolution. Our research presents an innovative, fully automated system called MadDog, which leverages advanced techniques in natural language processing to achieve efficient, real-time processing of documents containing dense textual information. MadDog combines the use of denotation-generating algorithms with the FastAPI framework to acurately interpret and resolve a single acronym within each noun phrase, taking into consideration the surrounding context. Our results demonstrate that the system can process a significant amount of information in a short amount of time, with the capability of resolving a substantial number of acronyms out of a given dataset. Furthermore, our findings reveal that user interaction can be minimized through the use of cutting-edge technology, with the system capable of acurately interpreting and resolving a significant amount of acronyms with a high degree of confidence.

Converting spin-polarized atoms into bound molecules with opposite spin is
achieved with remarkable efficiency through the FCHIRP laser pulse in a three-body
recombination reaction. The key to this highly selective process lies in the
reaction's ability to be controlled by a specific virtual energy state. By
adjusting the intensity of the laser, we can precisely regulate the conversion
rate between atoms and molecules. Notably, this process is not limited to
identical fermion systems but can be applied to a broader range of particles,
including bosons and Neumann-Entrop particles, and even mixture of two
different species of fermions. The discovery of this interconversion process
holds significant potential for the field of quantum simulation using tightly
confined gas ensembles.

Due to its high density, DNA synthesis has emerged as a promising storage technology, but certain aspects of the process, like hierarchy management and data updates, pose significant challenges. A novel hierarchical DNA storage scheme was proposed to tackle these issues, yet its effectiveness relies heavily on the efficiency of cross-storage operations. In this study, we address the limitations of this approach by designing two optimization strategies to minimize the corresponding operations. First, a hierarchy management method based on data usage frequency was introduced to better manage the hierarchical structure. Next, a DNA synthesis process that combines high and low-level storages simultaneously was proposed to reduce the operations required for updating data in multiple levels. Finally, a set of simulation results was used to demonstrate the proposed methods' ability to significantly improve storage performance and data update speed.

Topological insulators and semimetals have gained significant attention in condensed matter physics over the past decade. This review focuses on momentum-space structures known as nodal surfaces, which are characterized by a (d-2)-dimensional topology in d-dimensional space. These structures, which are related to nontrivial topological invariants, can be found in various forms including large Fermi surfaces in 3D and rings in 2D. We will examine their theoretical underpinnings, as well as their recent experimental realizations in 2D and 3D systems, including photonic crystals.

This project aims to detect and differentiate between glioma and non-glioma tumors using MRI scans, with an additional task of classifying non-glioma tumors into meningioma and pituitary adenoma. MRI images are used for this purpose, with a single patient often having scans in three different MRI modalities. We conducted a thorough analysis of MRI images to identify two main types of brain tumors, glioma and non-glioma, with the latter type further divided into meningioma and pituitary adenoma. We also explored a method to differentiate between non-glioma tumors. Our research involved a multi-task learning approach, with a focus on brain tumor detection and classification. We conducted a comprehensive evaluation of MRI images, with the dataset consisting of a collection of images from three different MRI modalities, with the dataset being publicly available.

Differentiable rendering systems enable the efficient calculation of shadow issues in inverse problems such as shape optimization. However, traditional methods using analytical solutions to Poisson's equation suffer from inaccuracies due to boundary approximations and limited effectiveness in handling complex light occlusions. In this paper, we introduce an innovative approach to shadow evaluation based on a differentiable solver with an iterative update rule that decouples boundary approximation errors. Our method is particularly suited for use in differentiable rendering frameworks and demonstrates significant improvements in accuracy and scalability. We further develop a light source decoupling technique to reduce computational costs and achieve near-kernel performance. Experimental results show our method's versatility and effectiveness in solving light occlusion problems of varying complexity, including applications in image completion and reflectance estimation.

A longstanding challenge in video acquisition remains deep interlacing, particularly problematic for high-resolution and fast-moving scenes.  This paper presents an innovative, instantaneous deep deinterlacing system that efficiently processes video without requiring memory proportional to the number of frames.  Our method utilizes a series of lightweight spatial convolution layers to generate multiple frames of reference, which are then interleaved and processed frame by frame to produce high-quality output.  This system is optimized for real-time processing on resource-constrained devices, achieving up to 30 frames per second on a mobile processor.  Our model outperforms existing deep learning deinterlacing techniques and matches the performance of the best available frame-rate-matched reference.  It also excels at processing scenes with significant motion.

The average square radius of the neutron distribution has been calculated for various nuclear models, with results shown for 120-128 nuclei across the spherical and deformed regions using the Stochastic Mean Field model.

To better understand and forecast natural disasters caused by water, such as floods and landslides, researchers focus on modeling the movement of flowing water using the shallow water equations. These models are based on the complex dynamics of water in motion, described by the Navier-Stokes equations. Despite their effectiveness, solving these models for real-world scenarios with detailed geometry and physical parameters is a time-consuming and computationally expensive process. To overcome this limitation, we developed an advanced computational model that can rapidly predict water flow by integrating numerical discretization with deep learning techniques. This model is capable of providing highly accurate results, as verified by extensive numerical experiments. To our knowledge, this is the first application of such a technique to predicting water flow in environments affected by natural disasters.

High dynamic range photography enables capturing a broader spectrum of brightness levels in a scene, exceeding the capabilities of a single image. Conventional methods, such as cue-based and pair-wise techniques, have their limitations in providing reliable exposure information and often necessitate user input. To overcome these limitations, a novel approach combining user-driven information with optimal exposure selection and image fusion is presented. Initially, a user-friendly interface is established to gather reliable exposure information from the user. Subsequently, an optimal exposure choice algorithm is developed to filter out inaccurate user input. Finally, a suitable image fusion approach is implemented to combine the exposed images. The proposed method's performance is validated through comparative studies and user feedback on mobile devices.

This paper presents key advancements in causal neural network research over the past decade. We begin by summarizing the basic concepts of causal representation and the primary frameworks of causal inference. Following this, we focus on unobserved causal representation learning and proceed to highlight recent progress in using causal representations for subsequent neural network applications. These areas include robust prediction, the interpretation of predictions, and planning. We then outline several prevailing challenges and potential pathways for overcoming them.

This research investigates temperature variations within a gas-solid bed as gas flows through it, utilizing high-speed MRI combined with a magnetic resonance thermometry (MRT) technique. MRI/MRT enables non-invasive visualization of temperature distributions in three dimensions, revealing distinct patterns that align with the arrangement of particles in the bed. Notably, random temperature fluctuations occur in the packed zone due to heat conduction among particles, whereas a different pattern emerges in the fluidized zone where particles mix freely. These patterns are essential for understanding and potentially enhancing the efficiency of industrial processes affected by heat transfer.

Mumford's conjecture suggests that the number of smooth curves within a specific cubic surface in three-dimensional space can be precisely determined by combining topological properties of the surface. In this study, we aim to confirm this hypothesis for certain cubics that possess a special type of singular point, specifically one where three tangent planes intersect at a common point. By leveraging recent findings related to the bipartite b-principle, we manage to prove a broader version of Mumford's conjecture, covering a broader class of cubics.

This paper compares three conditioning methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems using the hierarchical parallel geometric multilevel method. Specifically, we examine the effectiveness of multilevel preconditioners in accurately capturing the intricate geometry and material properties of the heart.

As the number of rows and columns in an $n\times m$ random integer array increases, with each entry chosen independently and uniformly from $\{1,\dots,k\}$, we investigate the behavior of its connected components under a equivalence relation. This relationship establishes that two numbers are connected if they share the same row or column indices.
